content: Night eating syndrome (NES) is a recognized eating disorder that has been formally identified since 1999. It affects approximately 1–2% of the population. NES is also classified as a sleep-related disorder. It is often confused with sleep-related eating disorder (SRED), but the two conditions are distinct. Unlike occasional late-night snacking or skipped meals, NES is characterized by persistent and ongoing behaviors. Individuals with NES may be unaware of their nocturnal eating episodes, although some report feeling that they cannot fall asleep without eating first. It is worth noting that falling asleep is often easier on a full stomach. For those who are aware of their night eating, there is frequently an emotional component, and the foods consumed are typically comfort foods. Symptoms and Behaviors: 1. Individuals with NES often skip breakfast and delay their first meal for several hours after waking. 2. They consume at least half of their daily caloric intake after dinner, often after 9 or 10 PM. This does not typically include dessert if one is eaten. Late-night eating episodes predominantly consist of carbohydrates. However, unlike binge eating seen in other eating disorders, the consumption is spread out over several hours rather than occurring in a single episode. 3. Many individuals with NES experience depression or anxiety, often linked to their eating habits. These night eating episodes are more likely to evoke feelings of guilt rather than pleasure or enjoyment. 4. People with NES frequently have difficulty sleeping and may suffer from insomnia. They are also more likely than the general population to engage in sleepwalking. 5. For NES to be considered a clinical disorder, the pattern of behavior must persist for at least two months. Treatment: NES is associated with weight gain. Studies have shown that up to 28% of individuals seeking gastric bypass surgery suffer from NES. While not all individuals with NES are overweight, approximately one in four people who are overweight by 100 pounds or more are believed to have this condition. NES is often accompanied by what sufferers describe as an uncontrollable desire to eat, which they liken to an addiction. Treatment frequently involves pharmacological interventions. The antidepressant drug sertraline (commonly known as Zoloft) has demonstrated some efficacy in helping individuals with NES manage their symptoms.
